definition: Destitute means extremely poor, lacking even the basic necessities of life.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word destitute. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know destitute should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wildfire moved so fast that hundreds of families fled with only the clothes they wore, left destitute overnight, without homes, food, or savings.
A needy family lacks enough money for comfort but still gets by, while a destitute one lacks food, shelter, and every basic necessity.
Destitute describes total poverty in daily life, and penniless sharpens it even further, meaning literally not a single cent remains.

Impoverished means made poor, often by forces that drained resources over time: an impoverished region, an impoverished family. An impoverished household may still have a roof and some income. Destitute is the endpoint: lacking food, shelter, and every basic necessity, with nothing left to fall back on.

Poverty-stricken describes people suffering under severe, grinding poverty, usually as a long-standing condition of life. Destitute is even more absolute, and often more sudden: it means stripped of the basics themselves, food, shelter, and savings, the state a disaster can leave a family in overnight.

Broke is the casual, everyday word for having no money at the moment, and it is often temporary: a student can be broke until payday. Destitute is far graver. It means lacking even food and shelter, not just cash, and no one uses it lightly.

Destitute means extremely poor, lacking even the basic necessities of life.
After three years of drought killed his crops and then his cattle, the farmer sold the last of his tools to pay old debts.
Destitute, he arrived in the city with nothing but a blanket and depended on a soup kitchen for his only meal each day.
The farmer has lost not just income but everything, food, shelter, and possessions alike, which is what separates being destitute from being merely poor.

Destitute describes total poverty, the loss of food, shelter, and every basic necessity, and it often appears in the phrase 'left destitute.' Indigent, a related word taught elsewhere in this unit, covers similar poverty in a more clinical, institutional register, as in official discussions of who qualifies for aid, while destitute is the more absolute and dramatic word.

For eleven years, Tomas Rivera kept the night shift at a cannery and a rented room above a bakery.
Then the cannery closed, the room went with the job — the owner's cousin needed it — and within six weeks Tomas was destitute: no bed, no meals he could count on, forty-one dollars to his name.
The intake worker at the shelter wrote the word deliberately.
Her form offered softer labels for people short on rent or behind on bills; none of them fit a man with nothing to fall back on.
What struck her was the speed.
Hardship, in her files, usually gathered over years.
Tomas had crossed from getting by to having nothing in a single season.
The shelter's first goal, she told him, was small: an address, a bed, one basic restored at a time.
